claims.source: Furthermore, no difference was identified in the number of BLBP+ RG cells (including proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ population) in the IV-VZ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: An increased number of both total BLBP+ and proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ cells was observed in the PWM of the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: However, an increased number of both total BLBP+ and proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ cells was observed in the prospective white matter (PWM) of the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum compared to controls (Figure 2A,A′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2A′.

claims.claim: Mitotic index was significantly increased in the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO PWM.
claims.source: More importantly, mitotic index, determined by the ratio of proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ cells to the total BLBP+ cells, was significantly increased in the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO PWM (Figure 2A,A′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2A′.

claims.claim: Nf1 specifically constrains the proliferation of astrocyte precursors in the PWM, but not multipotent RG cells of the IV-VZ in the E17.5 cerebellum.
claims.source: These observations suggest that Nf1 specifically constrains the proliferation of astrocyte precursors in the PWM, but not multipotent RG cells of the IV-VZ in the E17.5 cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential proliferation patterns observed in PWM vs IV-VZ.

claims.claim: The increased mitotic index was no longer detected in the more differentiated BLBP+ BG cells in the anterior folia at P0.5, but only in the posterior folia (IX and X).
claims.source: Unexpectedly, the increased mitotic index was no longer detected in the more differentiated BLBP+ BG cells in the anterior folia, but only in the posterior folia (IX and X) of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum where BG cells had not formed a rudimentary PC/BG layer at P0.5 (Figure 2B,B′,2C,C′; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B′ and 2C′.

claims.claim: An increase of cells with strong nuclear BLBP staining in the P0.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was identified, suggesting a persistent increase of proliferating BG cells into postnatal stages.
claims.source: Consistently, an increase of cells with strong nuclear BLBP staining in the P0.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was identified, suggesting a persistent increase of proliferating BG cells into postnatal stages (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BLBP staining data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: BLBP+ cells in the PWM still exhibited an increased mitotic index in the P0.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: Similarly, BLBP+ cells in the PWM, the precursors of WM astrocytes, still exhibited an increased mitotic index in the P0.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–D′′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D′′.

claims.claim: At P8, the mitotic index of BLBP+ BG cells was no longer increased in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, despite a significant increase of both total BLBP+ and proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ BG cells.
claims.source: At P8 when BG cells had formed a rudimentary PC/BG layer throughout the cerebellum, the mitotic index of BLBP+ BG cells was no longer increased in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, despite a significant increase of both total BLBP+ and proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ BG cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,E′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E′.

claims.claim: Nf1 constrains the proliferation of the BG/astrocyte lineage cells specifically at an intermediate precursor stage located in the PWM, but not at an earlier RG stem cell stage or a more differentiated BG stage.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that Nf1 constrains the proliferation of the BG/astrocyte lineage cells specifically at an intermediate precursor stage located in the PWM, but not at an earlier RG stem cell stage or a more differentiated BG stage, thereby identifying a window of susceptibility of astrocyte precursors to Nf1 mutation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the temporal and spatial patterns of proliferation defects observed.

claims.claim: Excess BG cells failed to form a similar PC/BG layer at P8, but were aberrantly distributed throughout the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellar cortex.
claims.source: At P8, control BG cells labeled by nuclear Cre staining formed a rudimentary 2 to 3 cell-layer lining within the APC+ Purkinje cell layer (Figure 2E). In contrast, excess BG cells failed to form a similar PC/BG layer, but were aberrantly distributed throughout the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellar cortex (Figure 2E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Cre and APC staining data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Some Nf1-deficient BG cells extended their processes from ectopic locations of the cerebellum including the WM, ML and IGL, accompanied by misalignment of the BG scaffold.
claims.source: Consequently, some Nf1-deficient BG cells extended their processes from ectopic locations of the cerebellum including the WM, ML and IGL, accompanied by misalignment of the BG scaffold (Figure 2E,F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GFAP staining data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claims.claim: All major defects observed in BG cells, GCs and Purkinje cells of the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum were identified at P8.
claims.source: Indeed, all major defects observed in BG cells, GCs and Purkinje cells of the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum were identified at P8, suggesting that these defects manifest during neonatal stages (Figure 2G–H′; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H′′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of P8 and adult cerebella.

claims.claim: Overproduction of astrocyte precursors during embryonic stages is the primary defect causing both glial and neuronal abnormalities in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: These results supports a model wherein overproduction of astrocyte precursors during embryonic stages is the primary defect causing both glial and neuronal abnormalities in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claims.claim: NCreER-targeted cells analyzed at P21 were restricted to glial lineage cells in both the control and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum with only one exception in folium X.
claims.source: Upon a single TM pulse at E17.5, NCreER-targeted cells analyzed at P21 were restricted to glial lineage cells in both the control and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum with only one exception in folium X, where a significant number of both glia and GCs in the IGL were targeted (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by β-gal staining data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claims.claim: No alteration in the number of BLBP+ cells or the BG scaffold was observed in any of the anterior folia (I to V) between the control and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: No alteration in the number of BLBP+ cells or the BG scaffold was observed in any of the anterior folia (I to V) between the control and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BLBP staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Neurons did not abnormally accumulate in the ML of the anterior Nf1NCreERCKO folia.
claims.source: Furthermore, neurons did not abnormally accumulate in the ML of the anterior Nf1NCreERCKO folia (Figure 3A,A′; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,D′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by NeuN staining and quantification data shown in Figure 3A′.

claims.claim: In folium X, the number of Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells (BLBP+β-gal+) was significantly increased in the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: In folium X, the number of Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells (BLBP+β-gal+) was significantly increased, though this was subtle compared to the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The other posterior folia (e.g., VI–IX) exhibited a slightly, but significantly increased number of Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells in the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: Indeed, the other posterior folia (e.g., VI–IX) exhibited a slightly, but significantly increased number of Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,C′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C′.

claims.claim: The overproduction of BLBP+β-gal+ BG cells in the posterior folia of the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum appeared to be caused by cell-autonomous Nf1 inactivation.
claims.source: The overproduction of BLBP+β-gal+ BG cells in the posterior folia of the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum appeared to be caused by cell-autonomous Nf1 inactivation, as the number of non-NCreER-targeted BLBP+β-gal- cells in the same areas was not altered (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only β-gal+ cells were increased.

claims.claim: The overproduction of BLBP+ BG cells was accompanied by focal misalignment of the BG scaffold and abnormal accumulation of both Nf1-deficient and Nf1-intact neurons in the ML of the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: Importantly, the overproduction of BLBP+ BG cells was accompanied by focal misalignment of the BG scaffold and abnormal accumulation of both Nf1-deficient (NeuN+β-gal+) and Nf1-intact (NeuN+β-gal−) neurons in the ML of the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum (Figure 3B,D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by NeuN and β-gal staining data shown in Figure 3B,D.

claims.claim: Overproduction of astrocytic lineage causes impaired formation of the PC/BG monolayer and BG scaffold, non-cell-autonomously arresting GC migration.
claims.source: These results suggest that overproduction of this particular astrocytic lineage causes impaired formation of the PC/BG monolayer and BG scaffold, non-cell-autonomously arresting GC migration.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Nf1-deficient and Nf1-intact neurons accumulate in the ML.

claims.claim: Math1-cre-mediated recombination was almost exclusively restricted to the cells in the IGL of the adult cerebellum.
claims.source: Math1-cre-mediated recombination was almost exclusively restricted to the cells in the IGL of the adult cerebellum (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: β-gal+ cells were restricted to GCs in the IGL, but not Purkinje cells or glial cells, including BG cells in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum.
claims.source: Double staining of β-gal and other lineage markers showed that β-gal+ cells were restricted to GCs in the IGL, but not Purkinje cells or glial cells, including BG cells (Figure 4B,B′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double staining data shown in Figure 4B,B′.

claims.claim: No defect in Purkinje cells or glial cells, particularly the BG scaffold, was observed in the adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum.
claims.source: No defect in Purkinje cells or glial cells, particularly the BG scaffold, was observed in the adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum (Figure 4B,B′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by staining data shown in Figure 4B,B′.

claims.claim: The Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum exhibited abnormal accumulation of cells in the ML including some on the pial surface.
claims.source: However, the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum did exhibit one major defect observed in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum—abnormal accumulation of cells in the ML including some on the pial surface (arrows, Figure 4A,B–B′′; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,A′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claims.claim: The increased neuronal density in the ML of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum was caused by abnormal accumulation of Nf1-deficient NeuN+ neurons in a cell-autonomous manner.
claims.source: The number of NeuN+β-gal+, but not NeuN+β-gal− neurons, was significantly increased, suggesting that the increased neuronal density in the ML of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum was caused by abnormal accumulation of Nf1-deficient NeuN+ neurons in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 4A,B,B′′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B′′.

claims.claim: Abnormal accumulation of neurons was evident in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, suggesting a developmental defect during neonatal stages.
claims.source: Despite that no defect in the BG scaffold was observed, abnormal accumulation of neurons was evident in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, suggesting a developmental defect during neonatal stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: 24 hr after BrdU pulse, BrdU+ cells in both the control and Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum remained exclusively in the EGL and exhibited similar cell cycle profiles.
claims.source: 24 hr after pulse, BrdU+ cells in both the control and Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum remained exclusively in the EGL and exhibited similar cell cycle profiles, suggesting that Nf1 is not required for proliferation and cell-cycle exit of GC precursors (GCPs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–C′′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BrdU and Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Nf1 is not required for proliferation and cell-cycle exit of GC precursors.
claims.source: 24 hr after pulse, BrdU+ cells in both the control and Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum remained exclusively in the EGL and exhibited similar cell cycle profiles, suggesting that Nf1 is not required for proliferation and cell-cycle exit of GC precursors (GCPs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–C′′).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similar cell cycle profiles observed.

claims.claim: 32 hr after BrdU pulse, many BrdU+ cells in the Nf1Math1CKO ML already acquired MAP2 expression with rounded nuclei—typical neuronal differentiation features for mature GCs in the IGL.
claims.source: However, 32 hr after BrdU pulse, a subset of BrdU+ cells in the control cerebellum started departing from the EGL and entered the ML, not yet reaching the IGL (Figure 4C). While migrating GCs in the control ML did not express MAP2, a marker for mature GCs in the IGL, and had nuclei with a spindle-shaped migrating morphology, many BrdU+ cells in the Nf1Math1CKO ML already acquired MAP2 expression with rounded nuclei—typical neuronal differentiation features for mature GCs in the IGL (arrows, Figure 4C,C′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BrdU and MAP2 staining data shown in Figure 4C,C′.

claims.claim: After 48-hr BrdU pulse, BrdU+MAP2+ cells in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum progressively accumulated in the ML and EGL whereas control BrdU+ cells did not express MAP2 until they reached the IGL.
claims.source: After 48-hr BrdU pulse, BrdU+MAP2+ cells in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum progressively accumulated in the ML and EGL whereas control BrdU+ cells did not express MAP2 until they reached the IGL (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,D′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BrdU and MAP2 staining data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Newly generated neurons were abnormally accumulated in the ML/EGL of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, leading to an increased number of differentiated BrdU+Ki67− and p27+ cells in the ML/EGL with a concomitant reduction in the IGL.
claims.source: Newly generated neurons were abnormally accumulated in the ML/EGL of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, leading to an increased number of differentiated BrdU+Ki67− and p27+ cells in the ML/EGL with a concomitant reduction in the IGL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,E′,F,F′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E′,F′.

claims.claim: A subset of Nf1-deficient GCPs undergo accelerated and premature neuronal differentiation, thereby arresting their migration in the EGL and ML.
claims.source: These observations suggest that a subset of Nf1-deficient GCPs undergo accelerated and premature neuronal differentiation, thereby arresting their migration in the EGL and ML.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the BrdU pulse-chase experiments showing premature MAP2 expression.

claims.claim: 2 days after being plated in culture, significantly more Nf1-deficient GCPs expressed MAP2 than control cells, confirming an accelerated neuronal differentiation rate in a cell-autonomous manner.
claims.source: This conclusion was further supported by in vitro studies. 2 days after being plated in culture, significantly more Nf1-deficient GCPs expressed MAP2 than control cells, confirming an accelerated neuronal differentiation rate in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,G′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro differentiation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,G′.

claims.claim: Nf1-deficient GCs could efficiently interact with wild-type glia in a co-culture system and migrated normally in a trans-well migration assay.
claims.source: Importantly, Nf1-deficient GCs could efficiently interact with wild-type glia in a co-culture system and migrated normally in a trans-well migration assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,H′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-culture and trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,H′.

claims.claim: Nf1 is indirectly required for GC migration by suppressing GCPs to undergo premature terminal differentiation and ectopic differentiation to Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in the EGL and ML.
claims.source: Thus, our study demonstrates that Nf1 is indirectly required for GC migration by suppressing GCPs to undergo premature terminal differentiation and ectopic differentiation to Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in the EGL and ML.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both in vivo and in vitro experimental data.

claims.claim: Many of the prematurely differentiated neurons in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed Tbr2, a marker specific for UBCs in the cerebellum.
claims.source: Strikingly, many of the prematurely differentiated neurons in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed Tbr2, a marker specific for UBCs in the cerebellum (Figure 4E,E′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining data shown in Figure 4E,E′.

claims.claim: Tbr2+ cells including the newly generated Tbr2+BrdU+ cells were readily identified in the P8 Nf1Math1CKO EGL and ML.
claims.source: While Tbr2+ UBCs were rarely identified in the control ML (Englund et al., 2006), Tbr2+ cells including the newly generated Tbr2+BrdU+ cells were readily identified in the P8 Nf1Math1CKO EGL and ML (Figure 4E,E′,F,F′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 and BrdU staining data shown in Figure 4E,E′,F,F′.

claims.claim: Tbr2 expression was ectopically acquired in a subset of newly generated cells even before migrating out of the EGL.
claims.source: Tbr2 expression was ectopically acquired in a subset of newly generated cells even before migrating out of the EGL, and over time these Tbr2+BrdU+ double-positive cells progressively accumulated from the EGL, ML to IGL (Figure 4F,F′,G,G′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 and BrdU staining data shown in Figure 4F,F′,G,G′.

claims.claim: Nf1 inactivation ectopically generates Tbr2+ UBCs from GCPs in the EGL, which appear to migrate along the same pathway as GCs.
claims.source: These observations demonstrate that Nf1 inactivation ectopically generates Tbr2+ UBCs from GCPs in the EGL, which appear to migrate along the same pathway as GCs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Tbr2+ cells in the EGL and their progressive accumulation in ML and IGL.

claims.claim: Cells with the classic morphology of UBCs were identified in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, but not in the control cerebellum.
claims.source: More importantly, cells with the classic morphology of UBCs were identified in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, but not in the control cerebellum, indicating that these Tbr2+ cells not only acquire UBC-specific Tbr2 expression, but also undergo morphological differentiation of UBCs (Figure 4H) (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Golgi staining data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Approximately 30–40% of abnormally accumulated NeuN+ neurons in the ML of the adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed Tbr2.
claims.source: Consequently, approximately 30–40% of abnormally accumulated NeuN+ neurons in the ML of the adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed Tbr2 (Figure 4I,I′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4I′.

claims.claim: Nf1 plays cell-autonomous functions in suppressing GCPs to ectopically differentiate into UBCs.
claims.source: Together, these observations identify cell-autonomous Nf1 functions in suppressing GCPs to ectopically differentiate into UBCs (Figure 4J,J′).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing ectopic UBC generation in Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum.

claims.claim: A dramatic increase of Tbr2+ cells was observed in the ML throughout the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, which was most evident in folia V/VI.
claims.source: Indeed, a dramatic increase of Tbr2+ cells was also observed in the ML throughout the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, which was most evident in folia V/VI (Figure 5A–A′′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining and quantification data shown in Figure 5A–A′′.

claims.claim: The increase of Tbr2+ cells in the ML (98%) and IGL (94%) of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was almost entirely contributed by UBCs that expressed a moderate level of Tbr2 as well as NeuN (Tbr2+NeuN+).
claims.source: The increase of Tbr2+ cells in the ML (98%) and IGL (94%) of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was almost entirely contributed by UBCs that expressed a moderate level of Tbr2 as well as NeuN (Tbr2+NeuN+) (arrows, Figure 5B,B′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B′.

claims.claim: Almost all UBCs in the control folium V expressed high levels of Tbr2, but no NeuN (Tbr2highNeuN−) and were mainly distributed in the IGL.
claims.source: Almost all UBCs in the control folium V expressed high levels of Tbr2, but no NeuN (Tbr2highNeuN−) and were mainly distributed in the IGL (arrowheads, Figure 5B,B′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 and NeuN staining data shown in Figure 5B,B′.

claims.claim: The number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs was not significantly different between the control and the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: It should be noted that the number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs was not significantly different between the control and the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the quantification data.

claims.claim: Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in the ML and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum expressed CRhigh at a significantly lower percentage (36% and 38%) than Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs (67%) typically observed in the IGL.
claims.source: CRhigh is a marker for a subset of UBCs due to its low expression in granule cells (Mugnaini et al., 2011). Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in the ML and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum expressed CRhigh at a significantly lower percentage (36% and 38%) than Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs (67%) typically observed in the IGL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,A′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A′.

claims.claim: The absolute number of Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs was similar in the ML of folium V between the Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: Importantly, the absolute number of Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs was similar in the ML of folium V between the Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, further supporting the notion that ectopic generation of these UBCs results from loss of cell-autonomous Nf1 function in the glutamatergic neuronal lineages (Figure 4I′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4I′.

claims.claim: Ectopic Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs were continuously generated in the ML and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum during postnatal stages.
claims.source: Similar to the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, ectopic Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs were continuously generated in the ML and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum during postnatal stages (arrows, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,B′,C,C′), well beyond the developmental window of the generation of control Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs (Figure 4J,J′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BrdU pulse-chase data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,B′,C,C′.

claims.claim: The Tbr2+ UBCs ectopically generated in both the Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum are different from those previously described in the normal cerebellum in 6 critical aspects.
claims.source: Together, these observations demonstrate that the Tbr2+ UBCs ectopically generated in both the Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum are different from those previously described in the normal cerebellum in 6 critical aspects: (1) the marker expression, Tbr2+NeuN+ vs Tbr2highNeuN−, (2) the low vs high percentage expressing CRhigh, (3) the location, ML and IGL vs IGL, (4) the developmental origin, precursors in the EGL vs RL, (5) the timing of birth, neonatal vs embryonic stages, and (6) the migratory pathway, EGL-ML-IGL vs RL-PWM-IGL.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the differences observed between the two UBC sublineages.

claims.claim: Two UBC sublineages exist in the cerebellum.
claims.source: Thus, we suggest the existence of two UBC sublineages.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed differences between Tbr2+NeuN+ and Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs.

claims.claim: The majority of GABARα6-negative neurons were Tbr2+NeuN+ cells in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: Importantly, the majority of GABARα6-negative neurons were Tbr2+NeuN+ cells, while no significant difference was observed in GABAergic neurons between the control and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E,E′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E,E′.

claims.claim: Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs are the major contributors to the non-GCs abnormally accumulated in the ML of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: These observations suggest that Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs are the major contributors to the non-GCs abnormally accumulated in the ML of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 1D–D′′).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most GABARα6-negative neurons are Tbr2+NeuN+ cells.

claims.claim: The number of Tbr2+ cells was significantly increased in the ML of the folium X of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
claims.source: As observed in the rest of mutant folia, the number of Tbr2+ cells was also significantly increased in the ML of the folium X of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 5C,C′; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C′.

claims.claim: The number of Tbr2+ cells was unexpectedly reduced in the IGL of folium X of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum concomitant with ectopic presence of Tbr2+ cells in the surrounding WM.
claims.source: However, the number of Tbr2+ cells was unexpectedly reduced in the IGL of folium X of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum concomitant with ectopic presence of Tbr2+ cells in the surrounding WM (Figure 5C,C′; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C′.

claims.claim: The Tbr2+NeuN+ UBC sublineage contributed to almost the entire UBC population in the ML of both the control (97%) and Nf1hGFAPCKO (99%) folium X.
claims.source: As in Folium V, the Tbr2+NeuN+ UBC sublineage contributed to almost the entire UBC population in the ML of both the control (97%) and Nf1hGFAPCKO (99%) folium X (Figure 5D,D′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D′.

claims.claim: Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs were indeed increased in the IGL of Nf1hGFAPCKO folium X, and thus the reduction of Tbr2+ UBCs was exclusively attributed to a decreased number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the IGL.
claims.source: Similarly, Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs were indeed increased in the IGL of Nf1hGFAPCKO folium X, and thus the reduction of Tbr2+ UBCs was exclusively attributed to a decreased number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the IGL (Figure 5D,D′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D′.

claims.claim: UBCs in both the Nf1hGFAPCKO WM and IGL were the Tbr2highNeuN− sublineage, which was normally located in the IGL of the control cerebellum with a higher percentage expressing CRhigh.
claims.source: Consistently, UBCs in both the Nf1hGFAPCKO WM and IGL were the Tbr2highNeuN− sublineage, which was normally located in the IGL of the control cerebellum with a higher percentage expressing CRhigh (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–B′′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–B′′.

claims.claim: The total number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs was almost identical when the number in the WM and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was combined to compare with the number in the IGL of the control cerebellum, suggesting arrested migration in the WM.
claims.source: More importantly, the total number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs was almost identical, when the number of the Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the WM and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was combined to compare with the number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the IGL of the control cerebellum, suggesting arrested migration in the WM (Figure 5D–D′′).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D–D′′.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the clinical context for NF1, noting that it affects 1 in 2700 newborns and is associated with cognitive and motor impairments, autism characteristics, and cerebellar abnormalities. The cerebellum plays critical roles in motor control, cognition, and social interaction.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C2, C11, C13-C18) are well-established clinical and epidemiological facts supported by appropriate citations. They provide necessary background knowledge for the study and are not contested findings.

results.result: The manuscript provides established knowledge about NF1 genetics (loss-of-function mutations in NF1 gene encoding neurofibromin, a RAS negative regulator) and cerebellar development (RG cells give rise to GABAergic neurons and astrocytes; rhombic lip generates glutamatergic neurons; developmental timeline of cerebellar neurogenesis).
results.evaluation: These claims (C9, C10, C12, C19-C26) represent well-established knowledge about NF1 molecular biology and cerebellar development, appropriately cited from the literature. They provide essential background for interpreting the experimental results.

results.result: Previous studies showed that Nf1 heterozygous mice exhibit no cerebellar motor defects and children with NF1 do not have general cerebellar dysfunction. The authors hypothesize that bi-allelic Nf1 inactivation during development is required for cerebellar pathologies.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. Claim C29 is a reasonable hypothesis based on these prior observations, setting up the rationale for the current study using conditional knockout models.

results.result: Using hGFAP-cre to target Nf1 inactivation in RG stem cells around E12.5, the authors show that Nf1hGFAPCKO mice display severe motor defects and disrupted cerebellar neuronal lamination. Purkinje cells remain Nf1-positive but are disorganized, indicating non-cell-autonomous effects. Purkinje-specific Nf1 deletion (Nf1L7CKO) produces no defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C41 are well-supported by experimental data including β-gal reporter expression, PCR analysis, behavioral observations, and histological staining (Figures 1 and Figure 1—supplement 1). The non-cell-autonomous conclusion is logically sound given that Purkinje cells retain Nf1 expression yet are disorganized.

results.result: In Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, the boundary between ML, PCL, and IGL is poorly defined with dramatically increased cell numbers in ML and reduced numbers in IGL. Total NeuN+ neuron numbers are unchanged, but their distribution is altered with over 20-fold increase in ML. 60% of ML neurons express GABARα6 (GC marker), suggesting failed GC migration from EGL to IGL.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C49 are supported by quantitative histological data (Figure 1A-D). The inference that GCs fail to migrate (C49) is reasonable given the redistribution of GABARα6+ cells. However, the claim of "over 20-fold increase" (C47) should be verified against the actual quantification shown.

results.result: Bergmann glia (BG) cells in control cerebellum form a PC/BG monolayer, but Nf1-deficient BG cells fail to form this structure due to excess numbers and mispositioning. There is strong correlation between BG abnormalities and neuronal patterning defects. BG cells retain ability to extend processes to pial surface. The authors propose that Nf1 inactivation overproduces BG cells, impairing PC/BG monolayer formation and BG scaffold alignment, which non-cell-autonomously arrests GC migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by BLBP and GFAP staining data (Figure 1E-G). The correlation (C52) is demonstrated visually. Claims C54-C55 represent a mechanistic model that is reasonable given the data, though the causal chain requires further validation (addressed in subsequent experiments).

results.result: At E17.5, no defects were observed in overall cerebellar structure, Math1+ precursors, Purkinje cells, or BLBP+ cells in IV-VZ. However, increased numbers of total and proliferating BLBP+ cells with significantly increased mitotic index were observed in the prospective white matter (PWM) of Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, suggesting Nf1 specifically constrains proliferation of astrocyte precursors in PWM but not RG cells in IV-VZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data (Figure 2A, Figure 2—supplement 1A-B). The differential effect on PWM vs IV-VZ is clearly demonstrated. The inference (C60) is reasonable given the spatial specificity of the proliferation defect.

results.result: The increased mitotic index of BLBP+ cells was detected in PWM at E17.5 and in posterior folia at P0.5 (where BG cells had not yet formed rudimentary PC/BG layer), but not in anterior folia at P0.5 or throughout cerebellum at P8 (after PC/BG layer formation). This temporal pattern identifies a window of susceptibility at an intermediate BG precursor stage in PWM.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by temporal analysis of BLBP/Ki67 staining at multiple developmental stages (Figure 2B-D, Figure 2—supplement 1D-E). The inference about stage-specific susceptibility (C65) is well-supported by the data showing proliferation defects only at intermediate stages.

results.result: At P8, excess BG cells in Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum fail to form proper PC/BG layer and are aberrantly distributed throughout cerebellar cortex, with some extending processes from ectopic locations. All major defects in BG cells, GCs, and Purkinje cells observed in adult cerebellum were already present at P8, supporting a model where embryonic overproduction of astrocyte precursors is the primary defect.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67, C69 are supported by immunofluorescence data at P8 (Figure 2E-H, Figure 2—supplement 1F-H). The model (C70) is a reasonable inference from the temporal progression of defects, though it remains a proposed mechanism rather than definitively proven causation.

results.result: Using inducible Nf1NCreERCKO with tamoxifen at E17.5, NCreER-targeted cells at P21 were restricted to glia (except folium X where both glia and GCs were targeted). No alterations in BLBP+ cells or neuronal accumulation were observed in anterior folia, but posterior folia showed increased Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells in cell-autonomous manner, accompanied by BG scaffold misalignment and accumulation of both Nf1-deficient and Nf1-intact neurons in ML.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C78 are supported by β-gal lineage tracing and immunofluorescence data (Figure 3, Figure 3—supplement 1). The cell-autonomous increase in BLBP+ cells (C76) and non-cell-autonomous neuronal accumulation (C77-C78) are well-demonstrated. This experiment elegantly shows that late-stage Nf1 inactivation affects only posterior folia where BG cells are less differentiated.

results.result: Math1-cre-mediated recombination was restricted to IGL cells (GCs) in adult cerebellum, with no defects in Purkinje cells or BG scaffold. However, Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum showed abnormal cell accumulation in ML in cell-autonomous manner (only NeuN+β-gal+ neurons increased), evident at P8.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 are supported by X-gal staining, double immunofluorescence, and quantification (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—supplement 1A-B). The cell-autonomous nature (C83) is clearly demonstrated by selective increase in β-gal+ neurons. This establishes that Nf1 has cell-autonomous functions in glutamatergic neurons independent of glial defects.

results.result: BrdU pulse-chase experiments show that Nf1 is not required for GCP proliferation or cell cycle exit (similar profiles at 24h), but by 32h post-pulse, Nf1-deficient cells in ML prematurely express MAP2 with rounded nuclei (mature GC features). By 48h, BrdU+MAP2+ cells accumulate in ML/EGL. In vitro, Nf1-deficient GCPs show accelerated differentiation but normal migration with wild-type glia, demonstrating that Nf1 indirectly regulates GC migration by suppressing premature differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C93 are supported by comprehensive BrdU pulse-chase experiments (Figure 4C-D, Figure 4—supplement 1C-H), in vitro differentiation assays, and co-culture/transwell migration assays. The conclusion that migration defects are indirect consequences of premature differentiation (C93) is well-supported by the combination of in vivo and in vitro data.

results.result: Many prematurely differentiated neurons in Nf1Math1CKO ML express Tbr2 (UBC marker). Tbr2+ cells including newly generated Tbr2+BrdU+ cells are found in EGL and ML, with Tbr2 expression acquired before migration out of EGL. These cells show classic UBC morphology by Golgi staining. Approximately 30-40% of ML neurons in adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum express Tbr2, demonstrating cell-autonomous Nf1 function in suppressing ectopic UBC differentiation from GCPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 are supported by Tbr2 immunostaining, BrdU pulse-chase, Golgi staining, and quantification (Figure 4E-J). The ectopic generation of UBCs from EGL precursors (C97) is a novel finding well-supported by the temporal and spatial distribution of Tbr2+ cells. The cell-autonomous conclusion (C100) is appropriate given the Math1-cre specificity.

results.result: Dramatic increase of Tbr2+ cells in ML of Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (most evident in folia V/VI) is almost entirely due to Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs (98% in ML, 94% in IGL), distinct from control Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs. These two UBC populations differ in marker expression, CR expression percentage, location, developmental origin, timing of birth, and migratory pathway. Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs are major contributors to non-GC neurons in ML.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C111 are supported by extensive Tbr2/NeuN/CR co-staining and quantification (Figure 5A-B, Figure 5—supplement 1). The identification of two distinct UBC sublineages (C108-C109) is a significant finding supported by multiple distinguishing features. The similar numbers of Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO (C106) supports the cell-autonomous mechanism.

results.result: In folium X of Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, Tbr2+ cells are increased in ML but reduced in IGL with ectopic presence in WM. The reduction is exclusively due to decreased Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs, while Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs are increased. Total Tbr2highNeuN− UBC numbers (WM+IGL) match controls, suggesting arrested migration in WM. No alterations were observed at early perinatal stages, but abnormal WM accumulation was evident at P8.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C120 are supported by quantitative analysis of Tbr2/NeuN co-staining in folium X at multiple developmental stages (Figure 5C-D, Figure 5—supplement 2). The inference of arrested migration (C117, C120) is well-supported by the redistribution pattern and temporal analysis. This demonstrates a non-cell-autonomous defect affecting the Tbr2highNeuN− UBC sublineage.

results.result: No ectopic Tbr2+ UBCs in WM of Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, suggesting non-cell-autonomous mechanism. Abnormally increased GFAP+BLBP− astrocytes in Nf1hGFAPCKO WM. In TM-induced Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum, Nf1-intact Tbr2high UBCs ectopically accumulate in WM of folium X, while excess Tbr2+ UBCs in ML are Nf1-deficient. This suggests excess WM astrocytes create physical barrier arresting Tbr2highNeuN− UBC migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are supported by comparative analysis across three mouse models (Figure 5E-G). The non-cell-autonomous mechanism (C125) is well-supported by the observation that Nf1-intact UBCs accumulate in WM where excess astrocytes are present (C123). This elegantly demonstrates glia-dependent migration defects.

results.result: Western blot analysis shows Erk/MAPK is the only consistently hyperactivated downstream pathway in Nf1Math1CKO cerebella, with robust increase in cultured GCPs. Immunostaining shows high p-Erk in IGL, low in ML, and absent in EGL of control cerebellum at P8. Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum shows robust p-Erk increase in inner EGL, ML, and IGL, including abnormally accumulated ML neurons, demonstrating Nf1 is major regulator suppressing Erk in migrating GCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C131 are supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data (Figure 6A-B). The specificity for Erk pathway (C126) is important for therapeutic targeting. The spatial pattern of p-Erk expression (C128-C130) correlates well with the differentiation defects observed. The conclusion (C131) is well-supported.

results.result: MEK inhibition (P0.5-P21) completely eliminated ectopic Tbr2 expression in ML and reduced abnormally accumulated neurons by over 60% in Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum. Rapamycin treatment had no benefit but caused adverse effects. This demonstrates Nf1-mediated MEK/Erk inhibition is the major mechanism suppressing premature differentiation and ectopic UBC fate adoption.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C135 are supported by MEKi and rapamycin treatment experiments with quantification (Figure 6C, Figure 6—supplement 1). The complete rescue of ectopic Tbr2 expression (C132) and substantial reduction in neuronal accumulation (C133) provide strong evidence for Erk-dependent mechanism. The negative rapamycin result (C134) appropriately rules out mTORC1 pathway.

results.result: Of 14 MEKi-treated Nf1hGFAPCKO mice, 9 (G-responders) showed significant rescue of neuronal accumulation in ML, while 5 (P-responders) showed marginal improvement. G- and P-responders were distinguished by presence/absence of rescue in BG cell numbers, BG scaffold alignment, mispositioned Purkinje cells, and arrested UBCs in WM. Both groups showed complete rescue of ectopic Tbr2 in ML. The difference lies in rescue of glia-dependent defects, possibly due to higher Erk levels in glia. Increasing MEKi dose to 20 mg/kg produced more consistent rescues.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C141 are supported by comprehensive analysis of MEKi-treated mice with correlation plots (Figure 7). The distinction between G- and P-responders (C138) is well-documented. The explanation for variable response (C140) is reasonable given the differential p-Erk levels in glia vs neurons (Figure 7E, Figure 7—supplement 1). The dose-response relationship (C141) supports this interpretation.

results.result: MEKi-treated Nf1hGFAPCKO G-responders maintained rescue of glial and neuronal defects at P45-P60 (1 month post-treatment). MEKi-treated mutants stayed significantly longer on Rotarod than vehicle-treated mutants and showed improved motor learning during 4-day training (unlike vehicle-treated mutants). Improved motor performance was maintained 1 month post-treatment, though motor learning rescue was lost. G-responders performed better than P-responders, correlating with cerebellar rescue. The persistence of anatomical rescue (C142) and motor improvement (C145) one month after treatment cessation is significant. The correlation between anatomical and functional rescue (C146) strengthens the causal link. However, the loss of motor learning improvement (C145) suggests some deficits are not permanently corrected.

results.result: The study identifies essential roles of Nf1 during early but not late cerebellar development. Mechanistically, Nf1 is required for BG monolayer/scaffold formation by controlling astrocyte precursor proliferation at specific stage, but dispensable for BG cells during late development and adulthood. Nf1 indirectly regulates glutamatergic neuronal migration by controlling timely differentiation and suppressing ectopic UBC differentiation. The timely requirement allows development of therapeutic prevention strategy with long-term behavioral benefits.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C152 represent the main conclusions of the study, well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence from four mouse models, temporal analysis, and therapeutic intervention. The stage-specific requirement (C148-C150) is demonstrated by comparing hGFAP-cre (early) vs NCreER (late) models. The mechanistic insights (C151) are supported by Math1-cre experiments. The therapeutic implications (C152) are validated by MEKi treatment results.
